Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem

When can we pull a uniformly convergent subsequence out of a family of continuous functions?

Two conditions do the job. First, every function stays inside one 📦 box. Second, all of them wiggle with similar gentleness. A diagonal argument over the rationals then builds a subsequence. It closes in everywhere at once. The power functions fail the second condition: they turn steep suddenly near 1.

For example, picture 30 🧑 friends walking across a playground. Everyone must stay inside the fence. Nobody may suddenly sprint. Then you can pick a group whose walks grow alike. One friend sprinting at the end ruins the group.

Let (fn)⊂C(K)(f_n) \subset C(K)(fn​)⊂C(K) be equicontinuous and pointwise bounded (KKK compact metric), converging pointwise on a countable dense set {xk}\{x_k\}{xk​}.

Prove by the ε/3\varepsilon/3ε/3 argument that the convergence is uniform on all of KKK, and deduce as a corollary that (xn)(x^n)(xn) has no uniformly convergent subsequence on [0,1][0,1][0,1].

∣fp(x)−fq(x)∣≤ε3+ε3+ε3=ε(p,q≥N, uniformly Cauchy)\lvert f_p(x) - f_q(x) \rvert \le \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} = \varepsilon \quad (p, q \ge N,\ \text{uniformly Cauchy)}∣fp​(x)−fq​(x)∣≤3ε​+3ε​+3ε​=ε(p,q≥N, uniformly Cauchy)

Show proof

  1. Given ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, equicontinuity yields δ>0\delta > 0δ>0: d(x,y)<δd(x, y) < \deltad(x,y)<δ implies ∣fn(x)−fn(y)∣<ε/3\lvert f_n(x) - f_n(y) \rvert < \varepsilon/3∣fn​(x)−fn​(y)∣<ε/3 for every nnn. Since KKK is compact, finitely many points xk1,…,xkrx_{k_1}, \dots, x_{k_r}xk1​​,…,xkr​​ from the dense set {xk}\{x_k\}{xk​} form a δ\deltaδ-net of KKK.

  2. At the finitely many net points, the pointwise convergence of (fn)(f_n)(fn​) itself becomes "uniform": each (fn(xki))(f_n(x_{k_i}))(fn​(xki​​)) converges, hence is Cauchy, so choose NNN so large that p,q≥Np, q \ge Np,q≥N gives ∣fp(xki)−fq(xki)∣<ε/3\lvert f_p(x_{k_i}) - f_q(x_{k_i}) \rvert < \varepsilon/3∣fp​(xki​​)−fq​(xki​​)∣<ε/3 for every iii (a finite intersection of tails).

  3. For arbitrary x∈Kx \in Kx∈K, pick xkix_{k_i}xki​​ with d(x,xki)<δd(x, x_{k_i}) < \deltad(x,xki​​)<δ.

    By the triangle inequality, for p,q≥Np, q \ge Np,q≥N, ∣fp(x)−fq(x)∣≤∣fp(x)−fp(xki)∣+∣fp(xki)−fq(xki)∣+∣fq(xki)−fq(x)∣<ε/3+ε/3+ε/3=ε\lvert f_p(x) - f_q(x) \rvert \le \lvert f_p(x) - f_p(x_{k_i}) \rvert + \lvert f_p(x_{k_i}) - f_q(x_{k_i}) \rvert + \lvert f_q(x_{k_i}) - f_q(x) \rvert < \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 = \varepsilon∣fp​(x)−fq​(x)∣≤∣fp​(x)−fp​(xki​​)∣+∣fp​(xki​​)−fq​(xki​​)∣+∣fq​(xki​​)−fq​(x)∣<ε/3+ε/3+ε/3=ε.

    Hence (fn)(f_n)(fn​) itself is uniformly Cauchy, so (fn)(f_n)(fn​) converges uniformly by completeness of C(K)C(K)C(K).

  4. This completes (⟸\Longleftarrow⟸): pointwise bounded + equicontinuous implies uniformly bounded (as noted in the first problem).

    Also, applying the diagonal extraction of the previous problem to any sequence gives a subsequence converging on the dense set, and applying steps 1–3 to that subsequence shows it converges uniformly.

    Hence every sequence has a uniformly convergent subsequence, so by sequential compactness in metric spaces the set is relatively compact.

  5. Corollary: (xn)(x^n)(xn) has no uniformly convergent subsequence on [0,1][0,1][0,1].

    Its pointwise limit is discontinuous — 0 on [0,1)[0,1)[0,1), 1 at x=1x = 1x=1. If some subsequence converged uniformly, its limit would be continuous (a uniform limit of continuous functions) and would have to equal the pointwise limit — contradiction.

    So {xn}\{x^n\}{xn} is not equicontinuous at x=1x = 1x=1, and not totally bounded either: the subsequence x4kx^{4^k}x4k is 7/167/167/16-separated — for a=4k<4ℓ=ba = 4^k < 4^\ell = ba=4k<4ℓ=b, at the witness point x=2−1/ax = 2^{-1/a}x=2−1/a we have xa=1/2x^a = 1/2xa=1/2 and xb=2−b/a≤2−4=1/16x^b = 2^{-b/a} \le 2^{-4} = 1/16xb=2−b/a≤2−4=1/16, so ∥xa−xb∥∞≥1/2−1/16=7/16=0.4375≥0.4\lVert x^a - x^b \rVert_\infty \ge 1/2 - 1/16 = 7/16 = 0.4375 \ge 0.4∥xa−xb∥∞​≥1/2−1/16=7/16=0.4375≥0.4.

    (Not every distinct pair is this far apart: ∥x−x2∥∞=1/4\lVert x - x^2 \rVert_\infty = 1/4∥x−x2∥∞​=1/4.)
